analysis.one_liner: Limits electric utilities to requesting one rate increase per year.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on September 4, 2025, and has had no further action since, with 3 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1978 federal utility law to add a new standard: each electric utility could request no more than one rate increase per year, once every 365 days. Under this law, states are required to consider whether to adopt the standard, though states can ultimately decide for themselves whether to enforce it. The bill has been referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electric bills, especially customers who have faced repeated rate increases in a single year. Limiting utilities to one rate request per year gives state regulators and customers a more predictable schedule and reduces the number of separate rate hikes that can stack up in twelve months. It also gives state utility regulators a clearer, federally recognized standard to point to when they evaluate utility rate filings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and small businesses paying electric bills

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a standard to the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 stating that each electric utility shall request no more than one rate increase per year.
Under that law, states must consider whether to adopt the standard for utilities in their jurisdiction, putting the idea of a once-a-year cap on the formal agenda of every state utility regulator.
A limit on the frequency of rate requests makes household bills more predictable and reduces the number of separate increases customers can face in a single year.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utility companies, which would lose the ability to file multiple rate cases in a single year. Utilities use repeated rate filings to recover rising fuel, maintenance, and grid costs on an ongoing basis; a once-a-year limit would slow that recovery and require them to bundle their needs into larger, less frequent requests.

drawbacks.text: The bill limits how often utilities can request increases, not how large each increase can be. A utility limited to one request per year could simply file for a bigger increase once a year, so customers' total bills might not fall.

A yearly cap reduces utilities' ability to respond quickly to sudden cost changes, such as a spike in fuel or natural gas prices, which could delay needed recovery or lead utilities to build in a buffer and ask for more up front.
The standard is one states are required to consider, not required to adopt, so the practical effect depends entirely on what each state's regulators choose to do.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real household problem — repeated utility rate hikes — but through a weak mechanism. It caps the frequency of rate requests rather than their size, and it only requires states to consider the standard, not adopt it. Customers who face frequent small increases would benefit; customers facing one large annual increase would see no change, and could even see a larger single hike. It is a modest, low-cost consumer protection whose real-world impact is uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has been since its referral, waiting for the chair to schedule a hearing or vote that has not come.

narrative.text: Representative Josh Harder introduced the bill in the House on September 4, 2025.
Three House Democrats cosponsored the bill.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced.
No further action has been taken on the bill since the referral; it has not had a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities are better off so far, since a limit on their rate filings has gone nowhere and nothing constrains them. Customers remain exposed to repeated rate increases, but the bill's fate is not yet final while Congress is still in session.

for.name: Josh Harder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote since it was referred on September 4, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters in the record are Democrats, and no Republican has cosponsored the bill; the committee that controls its fate has a Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would limit utilities to one rate-increase request per year, slowing their ability to recover rising fuel and infrastructure costs through repeated filings. Customers who face multiple increases a year would save; the utilities' flexibility to bill more often is what the bill takes away.

The bill adds a federally defined standard that state regulators must consider when weighing utility rate filings, giving them a clearer benchmark. It also constrains their flexibility, since a utility limited to one filing a year would bundle larger asks into single cases.

analysis.trajectory: Single-sponsor bills referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee rarely reach the floor without a committee hearing or markup, and this one has had no movement in months and no Republican cosponsors. The most likely path is that it stays in committee and expires at the end of this Congress, though the sponsor could reintroduce it in a future session.
